In contrast, the lazy/eventual consistency of a decentralized network converts hard correlated failures into soft degradation, making it more resilient to shared causes.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the large service is shown to use strong consistency for critical state but degrades to eventual consistency for non-critical paths, the distinction blurs.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If decentralized services are shown to have hard failure modes on shared dependencies (e.g., DNS, identity), the consistency model is not the primary driver of resilience.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a strict consistency system is shown to have a perfect consensus algorithm that is immune to the specific shared cause, the claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Building on SRC_005, a large service with strict consistency requires all replicas to agree; a shared cause (like a network partition) violates this, causing a hard systemic failure. Decentralized services using lazy/eventual consistency can continue operating locally during a partition. The shared cause does not stop the system; it only delays convergence. Thus, the consistency model determines whether a shared cause is a 'failure' or a 'degradation'. Decentralized networks are more resilient because they tolerate divergence during correlated events.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
